```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(data.table)
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
options(width=100)
out <- "outputs"
model_dir <- function(outcome) file.path(out,paste(outcome,params[[paste0(outcome,"_scope")]],"diagonal-primary",sep="-"))
lmm <- readRDS(file.path(model_dir("lmm"),"fit.rds"))
glmm <- readRDS(file.path(model_dir("glmm"),"fit.rds"))
if(file.exists(file.path(model_dir("glmm"),"fit_derivative_checked.rds")))
  glmm <- readRDS(file.path(model_dir("glmm"),"fit_derivative_checked.rds"))
d <- readRDS(file.path(out,"analysis_data.rds"))
contrasts <- fread(file.path(out,"planned_contrasts.csv"))
stopifnot(nrow(contrasts)==12,
          all(contrasts$scope[contrasts$outcome=="lmm"]==params$lmm_scope),
          all(contrasts$scope[contrasts$outcome=="glmm"]==params$glmm_scope))
predictions <- fread(file.path(out,"response_predictions.csv"))
diagnostics <- fread(file.path(out,"diagnostic_summary.csv"))
manifest <- jsonlite::read_json("data-manifest.json",simplifyVector=TRUE)
audit_lmm <- jsonlite::read_json(file.path(model_dir("lmm"),"audit.json"),simplifyVector=TRUE)
audit_glmm <- jsonlite::read_json(file.path(model_dir("glmm"),"audit.json"),simplifyVector=TRUE)
tab <- function(x,digits=3,caption=NULL) {
  if (!knitr::is_latex_output()) return(knitr::kable(x,digits=digits,caption=caption))
  x <- as.data.frame(x)
  names(x) <- gsub("_", " ", names(x), fixed=TRUE)
  weights <- vapply(x,function(z) if(is.numeric(z) || is.logical(z)) 1 else {
    n <- mean(nchar(as.character(z)),na.rm=TRUE)
    if(!is.finite(n)) n <- 0
    if(n>25) 3.5 else if(n>12) 2 else 1.2
  },numeric(1))
  weights <- pmax(weights,pmin(2,nchar(names(x))/13))
  # Reserve space for inter-column padding inside a 6.9-inch text block.
  widths <- (6.9 - ncol(x)*0.09)*weights/sum(weights)
  t <- knitr::kable(x,format="latex",booktabs=TRUE,longtable=TRUE,digits=digits,
                    row.names=FALSE,escape=TRUE,linesep="",caption=caption,label=NA)
  t <- kableExtra::kable_styling(t,latex_options="repeat_header",font_size=8)
  for(i in seq_along(widths)) t <- kableExtra::column_spec(t,i,width=sprintf("%.3fin",widths[i]))
  t
}
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) options(width=78)
```

## Purpose and interpretation

This analysis asks whether reading one's own discipline rather than the other
discipline is associated with different first-pass reading behavior, whether
that contrast differs between undergraduate and graduate readers, and whether
domain match modifies sensitivity to surprisal. Word length and lexical
frequency are included as additional lexical predictors.

This is an **exploratory, informed trial of a statistical skill**. The analyst
had seen the proposed evaluation criteria. There is no no-skill comparison and
no basis for estimating the skill's causal benefit from this run. The scientific
analysis itself is observational: discipline and study level were not randomized.

The continuous analysis uses `r format(nobs(lmm),big.mark=",")` fixated-word
observations (`r params$lmm_scope` word sample). The binary analysis uses
`r format(nobs(glmm),big.mark=",")` word opportunities
(`r params$glmm_scope` word sample). Both preserve all 75 readers and 12 texts.
The sampled-word fits use a seeded quarter of eligible word tokens within every
text, shared across readers. They must not be described as full-data analyses.

## Findings

{{< include findings.md >}}

## Data provenance and the observation unit

The inputs come from the [PoTeC repository](https://github.com/DiLi-Lab/PoTeC)
and its linked OSF word-level reading-measures archive. Git revision
`r manifest$github_revision` supplies the documentation and lexical features.
The separately downloaded OSF archive has its own SHA-256 in
`data-manifest.json`; the Git revision alone does not pin that archive.
The repository records a surprisal correction on June 17, 2026. Every selected
surprisal value in the archive was checked against the corrected pinned features.

The audit found **142,125 unique reader × text × word-position observations**,
75 readers and 1,895 word tokens. The roughly 404,000 count discussed in the
benchmark proposal belongs to a different, scanpath-level table. Treating
fixation-level repetitions as independent word outcomes would change the unit
of analysis.

```{r}
#| label: data-counts
tab(fread(file.path(out,"data_counts.csv")))
tab(fread(file.path(out,"reader_groups.csv")))
```

The upstream merge script fills missing lexical features with zero. The pinned
original word-feature files identify 115 words with unavailable lemma frequency,
corresponding to 8,625 reader–word rows. These were restored to missing and excluded
from this complete-covariate pilot. The remaining set has 133,500 binary-outcome
rows and 95,683 first-pass-fixated rows. This restriction changes the word population;
it is not evidence that lexical missingness is ignorable.

The analysis uses text-context GPT-2-large surprisal, chosen before fitting.
Log frequency, word length and surprisal are centered and scaled using **unique
eligible word tokens**, rather than the fixation-selected outcome rows.

```{r}
#| label: scaling
tab(fread(file.path(out,"scaling.csv")))
```

## Outcomes, design and estimands

For the LMM, the response is `log(FPRT)` among `FPF == 1` observations with
strictly positive FPRT. The audit verified that positive FPRT agrees with FPF.
Skipped words are not treated as zero-millisecond readings and no arbitrary
constant is added before logging.

For the GLMM, FPReg is modeled over **all eligible word opportunities**, including
zeros for words not fixated in the first pass. The audit verified that unfixated
words have FPReg zero. This outcome combines fixation opportunity and regression
propensity. It is different from the probability of regression conditional on
first-pass fixation; the conditional analysis is a sensitivity target, not an
interchangeable denominator.

```{r}
#| label: glmm-event-counts
tab(fread(file.path(out,"glmm_event_counts.csv")))
```

Each of the eight factorial cells contains regressions and non-regressions.
This rules out complete separation by those cells alone; it does not prove
absence of separation along every continuous predictor combination.

Readers are crossed with word tokens. Tokens belong to texts. Multiple words
also share a reader–text reading episode. Text domain and lexical covariates vary
within readers; reader discipline and study level vary within word items. A
by-word slope for word length or text domain would not represent within-word
variation. The support audit is retained in `outputs/design_support.csv`.

Numeric contrasts are fixed before fitting: biology = −0.5 and physics = +0.5
for reader discipline `D` and text domain `T`; undergraduate = −0.5 and graduate
= +0.5 for study level `L`. `S`, `F`, and `W` denote standardized surprisal,
log lemma frequency and word length. `TS=T*S` and `DL=D*L` are explicit numeric
random-effect columns.

For each study level, the domain-match estimand is

$$
\Delta_l=\tfrac12\{\eta_{B,l,B}-\eta_{B,l,P}
                       +\eta_{P,l,P}-\eta_{P,l,B}\},
$$

at the mean lexical profile. Reader disciplines receive equal weight, rather
than their unequal sample proportions. We also estimate
$\Delta_{graduate}-\Delta_{undergraduate}$, and the same three contrasts
of the surprisal slope. These are linear-predictor contrasts: log milliseconds
for the LMM and log odds for the GLMM. They are not probability differences.

## Model specification and computation

The fixed structure is

```r
D * L * T * S + (D * T) * (F + W)
```

This preserves the factorial hierarchy, includes study-level moderation of the
expertise–surprisal relationship, and allows domain-match dependence of the
length and frequency associations. Study-level moderation of length/frequency
is outside this pilot's fixed-effect specification.

The starting random structure is

```r
(1 + T + S + TS + W + F || reader) +
(1 + D + L + DL || item) +
(1 + D + L + DL || text) +
(1 | reader_text)
```

All double-bar predictors are numeric. This deliberately diagonal covariance
structure is a pragmatic restriction in the recorded contrast/centering basis.
It is not invariant to arbitrary recoding and is not claimed to be a maximal
model. Reader domain and domain-by-surprisal slopes protect the central within-reader
questions; item and text slopes represent reader-group variation within stimuli.
Only 12 texts inform the text covariance components.

The LMM uses REML. The GLMM uses a binomial logit likelihood with Laplace
approximation (`nAGQ=1`). Gradient and Hessian calculation was explicitly enabled;
installed lme4 defaults can omit derivative checks for large models. No
fixed-effect selection or significance-driven random-effect deletion was used.
The analysis plan and bounded computational policy are in `analysis-plan.yml`.

```{r}
#| label: model-audit
audits <- data.frame(
  model=c("Log-FPRT LMM","FPReg GLMM"),
  observations=c(nobs(lmm),nobs(glmm)),
  elapsed_seconds=c(audit_lmm$elapsed_seconds,audit_glmm$elapsed_seconds),
  singular=c(audit_lmm$singular,audit_glmm$singular),
  optimizer_code=c(audit_lmm$optimizer_code,audit_glmm$optimizer_code),
  derivatives_available=c(audit_lmm$derivatives_available,audit_glmm$derivatives_available))
tab(audits)
```

Optimizer exit codes are not adequacy certificates. The retained audits include
warnings, `VarCorr`, `rePCA`, gradients and Hessian eigenvalues. Boundary estimates
were retained and examined rather than removed until a warning disappeared.

Installed lme4 2.0.1 did not provide the singular GLMM's derivatives despite
`calc.derivs=TRUE`. The extra check reconstructs the same deviance function,
verifies its objective against the fitted likelihood, and explicitly evaluates
finite-difference derivatives. The original fit and original audit are preserved.

```{r}
#| label: explicit-glmm-derivatives
extra_path <- file.path(model_dir("glmm"),"explicit_derivatives.json")
if(file.exists(extra_path)) {
  extra <- jsonlite::read_json(extra_path,simplifyVector=TRUE)
  tab(data.frame(min_Hessian_eigenvalue=min(extra$hessian_eigenvalues),
    max_absolute_free_scaled_gradient=extra$max_abs_free_scaled_gradient,
    minimum_boundary_gradient=extra$minimum_boundary_gradient,
    elapsed_seconds=extra$elapsed_seconds),digits=6)
} else {
  cat("Explicit derivative check timed out after 900 seconds; no Hessian result is available. Numerical qualification remains unresolved.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: variance-components
tab(as.data.frame(VarCorr(lmm)),caption="Log-FPRT LMM variance components")
tab(as.data.frame(VarCorr(glmm)),caption="FPReg GLMM variance components")
```

The full coefficient tables below describe the recorded contrast basis. They
are not substitutes for the planned domain-match contrasts.

```{r}
#| label: fixed-coefficients
fixed_table <- function(fit) {
  data.frame(term=names(fixef(fit)),estimate=unname(fixef(fit)),
             SE=sqrt(diag(as.matrix(vcov(fit)))),row.names=NULL)
}
tab(fixed_table(lmm),digits=4,caption="Log-FPRT LMM fixed coefficients")
tab(fixed_table(glmm),digits=4,caption="FPReg GLMM fixed coefficients")
```

## Planned contrasts and inference

The LMM uses Satterthwaite approximate t inference through `lmerTest`; the GLMM
uses exploratory asymptotic Wald z inference with lme4's RX/PIRLS covariance
approximation. The explicit GLMM joint-Hessian calculation timed out, so these
GLMM intervals and p-values are numerically unqualified and are retained for
transparency, not as validated scientific inference.
Satterthwaite/Kenward–Roger corrections are not
applied to the logistic model. The twelve planned tests—six per outcome—form
one Holm-adjusted family. The displayed 95% intervals are **unadjusted**.
These are model-based approximations, not simulation-calibrated guarantees.

```{r}
#| label: planned-contrasts
display_contrasts <- contrasts[,.(outcome,contrast,estimate,
  `95% interval`=sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]",lower,upper),`Holm p`=p_holm)]
tab(display_contrasts,digits=4)
```

![](outputs/figures/lmm-contrasts.png){fig-alt="Log reading-time domain-match contrasts and unadjusted confidence intervals."}

![](outputs/figures/glmm-contrasts.png){fig-alt="Log-odds domain-match contrasts and unadjusted confidence intervals."}

## Response scales and observed data

For new-group predictions, the variance of the random linear predictor is
$v=zGz^\top$, summed across the fitted reader, item, text and reading-episode
blocks. A lognormal arithmetic mean is
$\exp(x\beta+(v+\sigma^2)/2)$. Simply exponentiating the log-scale expectation
does not produce that mean.

For the GLMM, the new-group probability integrates
$\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(x\beta+u)$ over $u\sim N(0,v)$.
Gauss–Hermite quadrature was checked using two quadrature sizes and independent
adaptive numerical integration. Setting random effects to zero instead yields
$\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(x\beta)$, a distinct target.

The curves below show **plug-in point estimates**, with estimated variance
components held fixed. They have no uncertainty ribbons and should not be read
as precise population curves. The contrast plots above display fixed-effect
uncertainty. A full interval for the integrated response mean would also need
to propagate covariance-parameter uncertainty. Solid curves integrate over
new-group heterogeneity; dashed curves set group effects to zero. For the LMM,
both arithmetic-mean curves include residual lognormal retransformation.

![](outputs/figures/lmm-predictions.png){fig-alt="Predicted first-pass reading time versus surprisal, by study level and domain match."}

![](outputs/figures/glmm-predictions.png){fig-alt="Predicted first-pass regression probability versus surprisal, by study level and domain match."}

```{r}
#| label: reference-predictions
tab(predictions[abs(S)<1e-10,.(outcome,level,match,zero_RE,integrated)],digits=4)
```

Observed reader summaries provide context without treating thousands of words
as independent reader replicates. These raw means mix lexical profiles and
are not the same estimands as the adjusted reference-profile predictions.

![](outputs/figures/lmm-raw.png){fig-alt="Paired observed reader mean first-pass reading times for own and other discipline texts."}

## Adequacy and sensitivity

```{r}
#| label: diagnostic-summary
tab(diagnostics,digits=4)
tab(fread(file.path(model_dir("glmm"),"conditional_simulation_checks.csv")),digits=4)
```

Adjacent-word residual pairs are formed only within a reader–text episode and
only where original word positions differ by one. Gaps introduced by subsampling
or missing covariates are not treated as adjacent words. Binary simulation checks
use 200 Bernoulli simulations conditional on fitted fixed and random effects,
without refitting. They probe residual structure at those fitted values; they do
not validate generalization or calibrate inferential error rates. DHARMa was not
installed, so these explicit checks are not labelled DHARMa results.

![](outputs/figures/lmm-qq.png){fig-alt="Q-Q plot of conditional LMM residuals."}

![](outputs/figures/lmm-residuals.png){fig-alt="Conditional LMM residuals against fitted values with a smooth trend."}

![](outputs/figures/glmm-calibration.png){fig-alt="Observed and fitted first-pass regression probabilities by in-sample prediction decile."}

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity
if(file.exists(file.path(out,"sensitivity_contrasts.csv"))) {
  sensitivity <- fread(file.path(out,"sensitivity_contrasts.csv"))
  tab(sensitivity[,.(model,contrast,estimate,`Shift / baseline SE`=shift_in_primary_SE)],digits=4)
} else {
  cat("Sensitivity results are documented in findings.md; no completed comparison table is available.")
}
```

Sensitivity fits are judged by focal estimate changes and numerical evidence,
not by which produces smaller p-values. Correlated reader/item covariance is the
prespecified structural alternative. A fixation-conditioned FPReg model, if
completed, changes the outcome population and must be interpreted accordingly.
Remaining sensitivity and adequacy limitations are stated in the findings.

## Reproduction and retained evidence

The document executes R to inspect retained fits and produce tables; expensive
fitting is separated into scripts so rendering does not silently launch hours
of refitting. The scripts and fitting formulas remain editable and reproducible:

```bash
python3 fetch_data.py
Rscript --vanilla prepare.R
Rscript --vanilla fit.R lmm full diagonal
Rscript --vanilla fit.R glmm quarter diagonal
Rscript --vanilla summarize.R full quarter
Rscript --vanilla sensitivity.R
quarto render analysis.qmd
```

Use the actual fit scopes and additional commands listed in `findings.md`.
Existing downloaded inputs are retained; verify `data-manifest.json` before
reuse. Re-running with a new download may produce different upstream bytes.
The prose findings describe this frozen run; substantive refits require reviewing
that interpretation as well as regenerating numerical tables.
The raw log and JSON receipt for each controlled run retain its exit status,
timing and command. No source skill or pre-existing repo edits were changed.
The CSV contrast table also retains standard errors, denominator degrees of
freedom, unadjusted p-values, interval limits and inference methods.

```{r}
#| label: runtime-versions
sessionInfo()
```
